## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{100}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can an accurate detection still be too late to guide a robot?_

A camera can recognize an obstacle correctly while reporting where it stood before the robot moved. Exposure, transport, and inference all consume time, while calibration error changes where the observation places the obstacle. The resulting claim must fit the remaining stopping clearance before it can support motion. Perception engineering therefore joins recognition quality to capture timing, spatial calibration, and measured error, including the conditions under which a sensor can no longer support its claim. At the causal boundary, an incorrect or stale observation can lead to irreversible motion, so the permission path needs evidence whose age and limits it can check.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Select sensing modalities by the physical quantity, coverage, and failure limits required for a spatial decision
- Diagnose exposure, rolling-shutter, and calibration errors before measurements enter a geometric estimate
- Calculate capture-to-dispatch age and account for continued aging through downstream consumption without double charging delay
- Evaluate whether qualified spatial error and stopping margins fit the available clearance
- Distinguish immediate occupancy evidence from persistent identity and learned semantic confidence
- Design an observation record whose timing, calibration, error qualification, and health checks support downstream use

:::

## Choosing Evidence for a Spatial Decision {#sec-perception-photons-to-claims}

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-opening-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OPENING SCENE: OBSERVATION AGE AT THE RACK END
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The opening paragraph of @sec-perception-photons-to-claims;
# │          also the temporal-batching paragraph and the clock-sync pitfall.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show how far the warehouse mobile manipulator travels while its
# │          navigation camera's observation of a person ages.
# │ Show:    t_age 51.6 ms; 77.4 mm of travel at the 1.5 m/s drive limit.
# │ How:     AISLE.perception_age and RM.base.max_velocity; displacement via
# │          calc_spatial_information_age_displacement.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class RackEndOpeningAge:
    """Travel during the navigation camera's observation age at the drive limit."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dx = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(v, t_age).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected t_age: {t_age}")
    check(abs(v.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected drive limit: {v}")
    check(abs(dx.magnitude - 77.4) < 0.05, f"Unexpected travel during t_age: {dx}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v.to(meter / second), unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    dx_str = fmt_length(dx, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
```

The warehouse mobile manipulator's vision model can recognize a person stepping out from a rack end almost every time and still hand the planner a position that is already out of date. The world keeps moving while the navigation camera integrates and reads out its image and while the pipeline processes it. On this machine, an illustrative `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.t_age_str` passes between the middle of the exposure and the moment perception dispatches the observation (derived in the latency waterfall of @sec-perception-latency-waterfall), and at the base's `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.v_str` drive limit the machine covers `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.dx_str` in that time. Recognition accuracy does not say whether that observation is fresh enough for the proposed motion. In physical AI, an observation has an expiration date.

The evaluation record limits where the learned proposer has evidence of useful behavior. Running that proposer also requires current evidence about the machine and its surroundings. Perception supplies this evidence as dated spatial claims across the proposal boundary of @sec-boundary-machine-model. It runs in the Brain, above that boundary, and holds no authority over the actuators; that authority stays with the deterministic permission path below it. Capture time, coordinate frame, and error qualification connect sensor physics to the clearance decision. Their meaning must be established before they can become fields in an observation record.

A vision-language-action (VLA) policy [@brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla], an end-to-end visuomotor policy without a language backbone [@zhao2023learning], and a modular estimator all need to relate the scene at capture to the machine at execution. Model topology changes processing costs but cannot eliminate exposure, readout, or transport. Explicit timestamps and transforms make that relationship inspectable; a hidden learned representation needs additional instrumentation or external checks. Neither organization makes a wet-floor reflection reliable evidence of open clearance.

The rack-end decision needs a bounded occupied region in the base frame before the remaining stopping clearance is consumed. Appearance helps identify a person; a bearing alone does not supply that region's metric range. The navigation camera therefore needs qualified depth or range corroboration before its detections support clearance. At the gripper, the required quantity changes again: visible shape can guide an approach, while contact deformation and slip require a sensor at the contact. Sensor selection starts with the physical quantity the action needs, then checks coverage and failure limits.

The comparison in @tbl-08-sensor-modalities shows what each sensing mechanism can claim and what must be checked before combining claims across an embodied sensor suite. A second modality can reduce a shared failure mode only when its own coverage, timing, calibration, and fault correlation are established.

| Modality         | Direct physical information                                                | Main limitation                                                                               | Permission-relevant check                             |
|:-----------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|
| RGB camera       | Bearing, appearance, and image motion                                      | Monocular depth scale is ambiguous; glare, darkness, and occlusion can hide objects           | Fresh capture time and validated metric corroboration |
| Active stereo    | Disparity-derived range with infrared texture projection                   | Sunlight washes out projected pattern; range error grows quadratically with distance ($z^2$)  | Range-dependent residual and bias validation          |
| Structured light | High-density triangulated depth from projected coded patterns              | Ambient solar infrared flooding; multi-robot pattern crosstalk; short range ($<3\,\text{m}$)  | Lighting lux limits and pattern decoding integrity    |
| Time-of-flight   | Metric depth via phase delay (iToF) or photon arrival timing (dToF)        | iToF phase wrapping; multipath reflections in corners; flying pixels on moving edges          | Ambiguity distance and corner multipath flags         |
| Pulsed LiDAR     | Metric time-of-flight range at sampled laser beam directions               | Near-field aerosol backscatter in fog/rain; retroreflector blooming; specular puddle dropouts | Qualified range, return quality, and scan timing      |
| FMCW radar       | Metric range and instantaneous radial Doppler velocity of targets          | Multipath ghost returns off ground; lower angular resolution; antenna sidelobe clutter        | Track association and coverage of crossing targets    |
| Event camera     | Asynchronous per-pixel log-intensity contrast events ($\ge C_{\text{th}}$) | Unchanging scenes supply little event evidence; noise and flicker can still generate events   | Event-rate health and independent metric depth source |
| Optical tactile  | Contact micro-depth, surface normals, and shear force vectors              | Zero sensing before physical contact; strictly localized to gripper elastomeric pad           | Contact threshold, slip flags, and marker tracking    |

: **Spatial sensor modality comparison**: Sensor mechanisms provide complementary but fallible claims across physical operating regimes. Numeric range, accuracy, refresh, and link budgets require a named device and mode. For example, [Prophesee EVT2](https://docs.prophesee.ai/stable/data/encoding_formats/evt2.html) encodes an event in 32 bits, so an event camera's link load scales with its event rate before transport overhead. {#tbl-08-sensor-modalities tbl-colwidths="[15,28,31,26]"}

On the running machine the division of labor is explicit, and it follows current practice for industrial mobile robots. The certified claim about a person at the rack end belongs to neither the camera nor the spinning LiDAR. ISO 3691-4 requires a driverless truck to detect persons in its path at performance level d [@iso3691part4; @tuv2021iso3691], the second highest of the five reliability grades, a to e, that ISO 13849-1 assigns to a safety function [@iso13849part1]. Mobile bases usually meet that requirement with a safety laser scanner, a planar time-of-flight device built and type-tested as an active opto-electronic protective device under IEC 61496-3 and rated at that level [@iec61496part3; @keyence2026szv]. The scanner reports only that something occupies its protective field, since its standard excludes classifying what it detects, and that report drives the certified stop path of @sec-enforcement-composite-budget. The base's OS1-64 LiDAR carries no such rating; its datasheet declares laser, product, and electromagnetic-compatibility conformance only [@ouster2025os1]. It supplies the dense metric range that the permission path checks against the rack-end clearance. That check is one of the permission path's unrated admission checks, a performance layer above the certified floor (@sec-enforcement-certified-functions), and its job is to keep learned proposals far enough from the scanner's field that the floor rarely trips. The navigation camera supplies semantics to the proposer: that the occupied region is a person rather than a tote, and where the person appears to be heading. The proposer builds its motion on the camera frame, so that frame's age is the evidence epoch the proposal carries, and we follow its capture pipeline through most of this chapter before dating the LiDAR against it in @sec-perception-lidar-age. This choice makes exposure, scan timing, and calibration load-bearing. The other modalities below explain when that choice must change: active ranging can supply missing range, event sensing preserves changing edges, and tactile sensing supplies contact evidence that a distant camera cannot observe.

## Capture Physics and Calibration {#sec-perception-transduction-calibration}

The navigation camera begins measuring a rack upright when light becomes charge at its detector. From transduction at the detector array to consumption by a policy backbone or state observer, every processing stage adds observation age. In CMOS image sensors, incident photons generate electron-hole pairs via the photoelectric effect with wavelength-dependent quantum efficiency $\eta(\lambda)$. Silicon photodiodes integrate this photocharge over a finite exposure duration $t_{\text{exp}}$, accumulating charge $Q = \int_0^{t_{\text{exp}}} \frac{q \eta(\lambda)}{h \nu} P_{\text{opt}}(t)\,dt$, where $q$ is elementary charge, $h$ is Planck's constant, $\nu$ is optical frequency, and $P_{\text{opt}}(t)$ is incident optical power. Photons striking the photodiode array do not instantly appear as feature embeddings in an inference engine; exposure, readout serialization, bus transport, memory transfer, preprocessing, and the vision backbone each take a share of the delay.

Because charge accumulates over the finite interval $t_{\text{exp}}$, the frame integrates scene radiance while the camera and scene can move. For approximately constant translation velocity $\mathbf{v}$ and angular rate $\boldsymbol{\omega}$, with the camera center offset by lever arm $\mathbf{r}$ from the rotation center, a conservative camera-center travel scale is:
$$\Delta x_{\text{motion}} = \|\mathbf{v}\| \, t_{\text{exp}} + \|\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}\| \, t_{\text{exp}}$$
This quantity is physical travel, not image-plane blur width. Projecting that motion into pixels requires the scene depth, focal length, viewing direction, and camera attitude change; rotation can blur the image even when the camera center does not translate. The resulting **motion blur** attenuates image gradients before feature extraction. A timestamp and calibrated transform locate the observation at its capture epoch, but cannot recover image detail lost during integration.

The finite integration window also determines which instant the image can represent. In an ideal linear response, the pixel records scene radiance $I(t)$ integrated over the exposure:
$$I_{\text{pixel}} = \int_{0}^{t_{\text{exp}}} I(t)\,dt$$

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-rolling-shutter-skew
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ROLLING-SHUTTER SKEW ON THE NAVIGATION CAMERA
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The exposure paragraph and the rolling-shutter example of
# │          @sec-perception-transduction-calibration.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the exposure-midpoint lag, per-row blur, and scanline skew
# │          the navigation camera records while the base passes a vertical
# │          rack upright.
# │ Show:    an 8 ms midpoint lag; 3,040 rows in 16.6 ms (5.46 us per row);
# │          24.9 mm of along-track skew and 24 mm of blur at the 1.5 m/s
# │          drive limit, about half of the along-travel allowance delta_loc;
# │          9.1 mm of lateral skew from an illustrative 0.5 rad/s yaw at the
# │          1.10 m rack-end distance, about 6 percent of the side clearance.
# │ How:     RM.nav_camera readout, exposure (a configured setting), and row
# │          count; RM.base drive limit; AISLE.delta_loc, AISLE.d_clear,
# │          AISLE.side_clearance; RM.imu sample rate for compensation.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_frequency, fmt_int, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class RollingShutterSkew:
    """Scanline skew and blur on the running machine's navigation camera at the drive limit."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: navigation camera)
    rows = camera.resolution_height  # category: datasheet
    t_readout = camera.readout_time.to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet
    t_exp = camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (configured exposure; low-light worst case, not a sensor rating)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    omega_yaw = 0.5 * radian / second  # category: illustrative (yaw rate while turning into the aisle)
    z_upright = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (range to the rack-end upright)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative (along-travel localization allowance)
    side_clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative
    f_imu = RM.imu.sample_rate  # category: datasheet

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_exp_half = (t_exp / 2).to(millisecond)
    t_row = (t_readout / rows).to(microsecond)
    skew = (v * t_readout).to(ureg.millimeter)  # along the direction of travel
    blur = (v * t_exp).to(ureg.millimeter)
    skew_over_loc = (skew / delta_loc).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    lateral = (z_upright * omega_yaw.to(1 / second).magnitude * t_readout.to(second).magnitude).to(ureg.millimeter)
    lateral_share = (lateral / side_clearance).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(rows == 3040, f"Unexpected navigation-camera row count: {rows}")
    check(abs(t_row.magnitude - 5.46) < 0.005, f"Unexpected row interval: {t_row}")
    check(abs(skew.magnitude - 24.9) < 0.05, f"Unexpected rolling-shutter skew: {skew}")
    check(abs(blur.magnitude - 24.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected per-row blur: {blur}")
    check(abs(t_exp_half.magnitude - 8.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected exposure-midpoint lag: {t_exp_half}")
    check(0.45 < skew_over_loc < 0.55, f"Prose says the along-track skew is about half of delta_loc: {skew_over_loc}")
    check(abs(lateral.magnitude - 9.1) < 0.05, f"Unexpected lateral skew from yaw: {lateral}")
    check(0.055 < lateral_share < 0.065, f"Prose says the lateral skew is about 6 percent of the side clearance: {lateral_share}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    rows_str = fmt_int(rows)
    last_row_str = fmt_int(rows - 1)
    t_readout_str = fmt_latency(t_readout, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_exp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_exp_half_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_half, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_row_str = fmt_latency(t_row, unit=microsecond, precision=2)
    skew_str = fmt_length(skew, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    blur_str = fmt_length(blur, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    omega_yaw_str = fmt(omega_yaw.to(radian / second).magnitude, precision=1)
    z_upright_str = fmt_length(z_upright.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc.to(ureg.millimeter), unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    lateral_str = fmt_length(lateral, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    lateral_pct_str = fmt_percent(lateral_share, precision=1)
    side_clearance_str = fmt_length(side_clearance.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    f_imu_str = fmt_frequency(f_imu, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0, commas=True)
```

For relative translation at speed $v$, the scene displacement during exposure is $\Delta x_{\text{motion}} = v\,t_{\text{exp}}$. Its image-plane blur depends on the projection geometry. Because charge accumulates across the whole window, the time the accumulated image represents is the exposure midpoint, $t_{\text{exp}}/2$ after exposure starts and the same interval before it ends. With the navigation camera's `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_exp_str` exposure at the base's `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str` drive limit, the image does not record where the robot *is*. It records where the robot *was* `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_exp_half_str` earlier, with `{python} RollingShutterSkew.blur_str` of relative translation during the exposure. The exposure is a configured setting, not a property of the sensor. The running machine carries this long exposure as its low-light worst case; a brighter aisle permits a shorter one, and both the blur and the midpoint lag shrink in proportion.

### Rolling shutter distortion and motion compensation

The exposure window schedule across the pixel array determines the spatial geometry of the image. In a **global shutter**\index{Global shutter!definition} sensor, every pixel photodiode accumulates charge during the identical time interval and transfers the accumulated electrons to shielded storage nodes simultaneously. In a **rolling shutter**\index{Rolling shutter!definition} sensor, silicon area and cost constraints dictate that rows are reset, exposed, and read out sequentially from the top scanline $y = 0$ to the bottom scanline $y = H - 1$. Each successive scanline begins exposure after a row period $t_{\text{row}}$, creating a progressive temporal offset across the image plane:[^fn-hw-rolling-shutter]
$$t(y) = t_{\text{start}} + y \cdot t_{\text{row}}$$
where $t_{\text{start}}$ is the start of exposure for the top row. When the body translates at linear velocity $v$ perpendicular to a vertical feature, scanline $y$ captures it at a spatial displacement:
$$\Delta x(y) = v \cdot y \cdot t_{\text{row}}$$

[^fn-hw-rolling-shutter]: **Rolling shutter epipolar geometry**\index{Hardware!rolling shutter}: Rolling shutter CMOS image sensors reset, integrate, and read pixel scanlines sequentially across the array rather than exposing all photosites simultaneously. When the camera rotates during this readout interval, straight physical edges project into curved geometric arcs across the image plane. This progressive scanline skew violates rigid multi-view epipolar constraints, which restrict a matched scene point in one view to its corresponding line in the other, causing visual backbones, depth networks, and odometry pipelines to compute spurious feature depths unless continuous-time scanline motion compensation or trajectory interpolation rectifies the frame before feature extraction.

Under rotational motion, rolling shutter distortion becomes non-linear. If the camera undergoes angular rotation at angular velocity vector $\boldsymbol{\omega} = [\omega_x, \omega_y, \omega_z]^T$ (e.g., rapid yaw or pitch during aggressive robot maneuvers), the effective camera attitude changes continuously as scanlines are read. Physically, the camera points in a slightly different direction for every single row. For a scanline at vertical coordinate $y$, the differential rotation relative to the frame start is $\Delta \boldsymbol{\theta}(y) \approx \boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot y \cdot t_{\text{row}}$. This scanline-dependent rotation warps straight physical lines into curves, stretches or compresses the image vertically during pitch, and shears vertical walls into slanted surfaces, as demonstrated by the propeller blade curvature in @fig-rolling-shutter-skew.

Consider the mobile manipulator's navigation camera while the base passes a vertical rack upright at its `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str` drive limit. The rolling shutter reads the frame's `{python} RollingShutterSkew.rows_str` rows in $t_{\text{readout}} =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_readout_str`, so the inter-row interval is $t_{\text{row}} =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_row_str`. An upright spanning the full height of the frame does not appear vertical in the captured array. The bottom scanline ($y =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.last_row_str`) is sampled `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_readout_str` after the top scanline ($y = 0$), producing a total spatial skew $\Delta x = v\,t_{\text{readout}}$ of `{python} RollingShutterSkew.skew_str`.

That skew lies along the direction of travel. The bottom rows see the upright from a camera position `{python} RollingShutterSkew.skew_str` farther down the aisle than the top rows did, so an image treated as an instantaneous rigid projection places the upright's lower half nearer than its upper half. The error therefore belongs with the stopping budget's localization allowance $\delta_{\text{loc}}$, which that budget holds along the direction of travel, and uncorrected it would spend about half of the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.delta_loc_str` allowance. The allowance assumes the skew has been removed before the estimator sees the frame. The side clearance faces a different term. A lateral rolling-shutter error comes from yaw: while the base turns at an illustrative `{python} RollingShutterSkew.omega_yaw_str` rad/s, the camera's bearing rotates by $\omega\,t_{\text{readout}}$ during readout, which at the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.z_upright_str` rack-end distance moves the upright sideways by $z\,\omega\,t_{\text{readout}} =$ `{python} RollingShutterSkew.lateral_str`, about `{python} RollingShutterSkew.lateral_pct_str` percent of the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.side_clearance_str` side clearance. Both terms scale with readout time. A global-shutter sensor, such as the machine's wrist camera, removes them at the cost of pixel area, so shutter type is a selection decision for any camera whose geometry feeds a clearance claim; this machine keeps the rolling-shutter navigation camera as the harder teaching case. Correcting this distortion requires **rolling-shutter motion compensation**\index{Rolling-shutter motion compensation!definition}, geometric unwarping using a camera pose for each scanline. The IMU supplies high-rate (`{python} RollingShutterSkew.f_imu_str`) angular-rate and specific-force measurements, not linear velocity. A state estimator combines those measurements with its initial state, bias and gravity estimates, and other available motion evidence to estimate body pose and velocity. Applying the calibrated body-to-camera extrinsics gives the instantaneous camera pose for each row, which permits scanline rectification before triangulation within the pose estimate's error bounds.

@Fig-08-rolling-shutter-rows plots that sampling against the row index: each row sees the upright from its own camera position, and each row's exposure smears the scene over its own interval.

::: {#fig-08-rolling-shutter-rows fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Row-by-row sampling on the navigation camera**: At the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str` drive limit, each of the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.rows_str` rows is read `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_row_str` after the one above it, so the bottom row sees the rack upright from a camera position `{python} RollingShutterSkew.skew_str` farther down the aisle than the top row (solid line; upper axis gives the read time). The shaded band is each row's own motion blur, `{python} RollingShutterSkew.blur_str` over the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.t_exp_str` exposure. Uncorrected, the skew alone spends about half of the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.delta_loc_str` localization allowance (dashed line)." fig-alt="Line plot with image row on the vertical axis, zero at the top, and camera position along the direction of travel in millimeters on the horizontal axis, with read time in milliseconds on a second axis above. A straight line runs from zero at the top row to about 25 millimeters at the bottom row, inside a shaded band about 24 millimeters wide. A dashed vertical line at 50 millimeters marks the localization allowance."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-perception-rolling-shutter-rows
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ROLLING-SHUTTER ROW SAMPLING (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-08-rolling-shutter-rows in
# │          @sec-perception-transduction-calibration.
# │
# │ Goal:    Make the along-travel skew physical: row index against the camera
# │          position at which that row was read, with per-row blur and the
# │          localization allowance it spends.
# │ Show:    0 -> 24.9 mm over 3,040 rows (16.6 ms); 24 mm blur band; 50 mm
# │          delta_loc line.
# │ How:     Reads RollingShutterSkew only; the plotted endpoint is guarded
# │          against its skew.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check

RS = RollingShutterSkew
PETROL, PINE, SOFT = "#007A87", "#1A4D3E", "#4A5568"  # measured, structural, neutral (theme-colors.tex)

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_rows = RS.rows
v_mm_per_ms = RS.v.to(ureg.millimeter / millisecond).magnitude
t_row_ms = RS.t_row.to(millisecond).magnitude
blur_mm = RS.blur.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude
dloc_mm = RS.delta_loc.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rows_axis = np.array([0.0, n_rows - 1.0])
x_cam = v_mm_per_ms * t_row_ms * rows_axis

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(v_mm_per_ms * t_row_ms * n_rows - RS.skew.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6, "The plotted skew must equal v * t_readout.")
check(RS.skew.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude < dloc_mm, "The skew must sit inside the drawn allowance.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(5.2, 2.7))
ax.fill_betweenx(rows_axis, x_cam - blur_mm / 2, x_cam + blur_mm / 2, color=PETROL, alpha=0.14, lw=0)
ax.plot(x_cam, rows_axis, color=PETROL, lw=2.0)
ax.axvline(dloc_mm, color=PINE, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (4, 3)))
ax.text(dloc_mm - 1, n_rows * 0.08, rf"$\delta_{{\mathrm{{loc}}}}$ = {RS.delta_loc_str}", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=8, color=PINE)
ax.annotate(
    f"skew {RS.skew_str}",
    xy=(x_cam[-1], rows_axis[-1]),
    xytext=(x_cam[-1] + 6, n_rows * 0.72),
    fontsize=8,
    color=PETROL,
    va="center",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=SOFT, lw=0.6),
)
ax.text(-blur_mm / 2 + 0.5, n_rows * 0.18, f"blur {RS.blur_str}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8, color=SOFT)
ax.set_xlim(-blur_mm / 2 - 2, dloc_mm + 6)
ax.set_ylim(n_rows * 1.03, -n_rows * 0.03)
ax.set_xlabel("camera position along travel when the row is read (mm)", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("image row", fontsize=9)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
top = ax.secondary_xaxis("top", functions=(lambda x: x / v_mm_per_ms, lambda t: t * v_mm_per_ms))
top.set_xlabel("read time after the top row (ms)", fontsize=9)
top.tick_params(labelsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

::: {#fig-rolling-shutter-skew fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Rolling shutter distortion geometry**: A phone camera's rolling shutter photographs a turning aircraft propeller. Because scanlines are exposed and read sequentially from top to bottom rather than simultaneously, blades that move appreciably during the frame's readout are recorded as curved, disconnected arcs; each row samples the blade at a later instant. On a moving robot the same row-by-row sampling shears straight structures and biases the geometry downstream estimators triangulate. (Credit: [Dick Lyon](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Propellor_with_rolling-shutter_artifact.jpg) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)." fig-alt="Photograph from an aircraft window of a propeller and engine nacelle in flight, with sky and ground below. The blades appear as bent, curved shapes, some detached from the hub, instead of straight radial blades."}
![](images/jpg/fig08_real_rolling_shutter_skew.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

The distorted blades in @fig-rolling-shutter-skew show why the correction must precede geometric interpretation. A learned feature extractor can also mistake scanline deformation for object shape; a stereo matcher can lose correspondences when they move off the expected epipolar line. Increasing model capacity does not restore the common capture geometry that those computations assume.

### Camera calibration

Rolling-shutter compensation assumes that the camera's geometry is already known, and every metric claim the camera supports rests on that calibration. Under the **pinhole camera model**\index{Pinhole camera model} [@hartley2003multiple], the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ maps a point $\mathbf{P}_c = [X_c, Y_c, Z_c]^\top$ in the camera's optical frame to the pixel $[u, v]^\top$:
$$\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \sim \frac{1}{Z_c} \mathbf{K} \mathbf{P}_c = \frac{1}{Z_c} \begin{bmatrix} f_x & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X_c \\ Y_c \\ Z_c \end{bmatrix}$$ {#eq-percep-pinhole-projection}
where $f_x, f_y$ are focal lengths in pixels and $(c_x, c_y)$ is the principal point. Inverting the map recovers only a bearing ray, along which every depth is consistent with the pixel:
$$\mathbf{r}(u, v) = \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{u - c_x}{f_x} \\ \frac{v - c_y}{f_y} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ {#eq-percep-bearing-ray}

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-capture-timing-scale
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CAPTURE-TIMING AND ATTITUDE ERROR SCALES AT THE RACK END
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The bearing-ray paragraph and the hardware-trigger paragraph of
# │          @sec-perception-transduction-calibration.
# │
# │ Goal:    Put machine-scale numbers on timing and attitude errors: travel per
# │          millisecond of misdating, lateral error per degree at the rack end,
# │          the travel hidden by an uncorrected exposure-start trigger stamp,
# │          and the lateral error per millisecond of stamp jitter while turning.
# │ Show:    1.5 mm per ms; 19.2 mm per degree at 1.10 m; 8 ms and 12 mm for
# │          the trigger correction; 0.5 mrad and 0.55 mm per ms of jitter.
# │ How:     RM.base drive limit; AISLE.d_clear; RM.nav_camera exposure;
# │          the illustrative yaw rate of RollingShutterSkew.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_angle, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class CaptureTimingScale:
    """Machine-scale travel and lever-arm errors from timing and attitude offsets."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    z = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end distance)
    t_exp = RM.nav_camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (configured exposure)
    omega_yaw = RollingShutterSkew.omega_yaw  # category: illustrative (yaw rate)
    dt_unit = 1.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (one millisecond of error)
    theta_unit = 1.0 * ureg.degree  # category: illustrative (one degree of error)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dx_per_ms = (v * dt_unit).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dy_per_deg = (z * math.sin(theta_unit.to(radian).magnitude)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    t_trigger_corr = (t_exp / 2).to(millisecond)
    dx_trigger = (v * t_trigger_corr).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dtheta_per_ms = (omega_yaw * dt_unit).to(ureg.milliradian)
    dy_per_ms_jitter = (z * dtheta_per_ms.to(radian).magnitude).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dx_per_ms.magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected travel per ms: {dx_per_ms}")
    check(abs(dy_per_deg.magnitude - 19.2) < 0.05, f"Unexpected lateral error per degree: {dy_per_deg}")
    check(abs(dx_trigger.magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected trigger-correction travel: {dx_trigger}")
    check(abs(dy_per_ms_jitter.magnitude - 0.55) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected lateral error per ms of jitter: {dy_per_ms_jitter}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    z_str = fmt_length(z.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    dx_per_ms_str = fmt_length(dx_per_ms, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    dy_per_deg_str = fmt_length(dy_per_deg, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    t_trigger_corr_str = fmt_latency(t_trigger_corr, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dx_trigger_str = fmt_length(dx_trigger, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    dtheta_per_ms_str = fmt_angle(dtheta_per_ms, unit=ureg.milliradian, precision=1)
    dy_per_ms_jitter_str = fmt_length(dy_per_ms_jitter, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
```

Critically, this bearing ray originates at the camera's optical center at the exact instant of photon exposure $t_0$. If downstream planning unprojects $\mathbf{r}(u, v)$ from the robot's *current* pose rather than its historical capture pose, the elapsed observation age $t_{\text{age}}$ translates the ray origin by $\Delta \mathbf{x} = \int_{t_0}^{t_0+t_{\text{age}}} \mathbf{v}(t)\,dt$. The two error sources scale differently on this machine. Each millisecond of unmodeled age moves the ray origin `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dx_per_ms_str` at the `{python} CaptureTimingScale.v_str` drive limit, so the full `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.t_age_str` age is `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.dx_str`. Each degree of attitude error instead moves a point at the `{python} CaptureTimingScale.z_str` rack-end distance `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dy_per_deg_str` sideways, and the lever arm grows with range. Either error can move a rack upright outside the envelope a collision checker tests. Metric depth must therefore come from stereo disparity, a range sensor, or a learned prior, each with its own error, and @sec-perception-error-clearance charges that error against the clearance. Lens distortion is rectified in the image signal processor stage of @tbl-08-latency-budget. The projection's derivation, the distortion model, and Zhang's planar calibration [@zhang2000flexible] are developed in @sec-appendix-systems-vision.

The camera's relation to the inertial measurement unit must be calibrated in space and in time together [@furgale2013unified]. An extrinsic rotation error $\theta$ misplaces a point at range $z$ by about $z\,\theta$, and the camera's offset from the inertial unit adds lever-arm accelerations (@sec-appendix-control-spatial). An uncalibrated offset $\Delta t$ between exposure and the inertial sample misorients the camera by $\omega\,\Delta t$ while the base turns at angular velocity $\omega$, misplacing the same point by about $z\,\omega\,\Delta t$, so the timing error grows with both turn rate and range. Latching exposure starts and inertial samples on one hardware trigger bounds that offset, leaving a residual that online calibration estimates. Each of these calibrations holds only inside the conditions under which it was fitted, which is why the observation record carries a calibration revision and its validity range.

Bounding the temporal offset $\Delta t$ means stamping the capture in hardware rather than when a software thread first sees the frame. A software stamp inherits operating-system scheduling jitter whose size depends on the platform and must be measured on it; while the base turns at `{python} RollingShutterSkew.omega_yaw_str` rad/s, each millisecond of that jitter misorients the camera by `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dtheta_per_ms_str`, or `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dy_per_ms_jitter_str` at the rack-end distance. Two hardware designs remove the jitter. In the first, one GPIO strobe (FSYNC) from the IMU's microcontroller both latches an inertial sample and starts the camera exposure. That edge marks the start of the first row's exposure, not the capture epoch, so the record must add $t_{\text{exp}}/2$ to reach the exposure midpoint, plus $y\,t_{\text{row}}$ for the row $y$ the claim represents. Omitting the correction dates the navigation camera's frame `{python} CaptureTimingScale.t_trigger_corr_str` early, `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dx_trigger_str` of travel at the drive limit, and because auto-exposure can change $t_{\text{exp}}$ from frame to frame, the correction must use the exposure the sensor reports for that frame. In the second design, used by networked sensors such as the machine's LiDAR and Ethernet cameras, each device stamps its own samples on a local clock that the Precision Time Protocol [@ieee15882019], or its time-sensitive-networking profile gPTP [@ieee8021as2020], disciplines to a network master. @Sec-perception-qualifying-error shows how the resulting clock error is measured.

### Choosing metric depth for the aisle

The navigation camera's bearing ray leaves range undetermined. Active optical depth can supply that missing measurement, but the warehouse's lighting, surface finish, and neighboring emitters determine which mechanism remains usable.

**Structured light**\index{Structured light!transduction} projects a known pattern and triangulates its deformation using a camera displaced from the projector. It adds texture to otherwise featureless cartons, but sunlight can wash out the pattern and overlapping projectors can corrupt correspondence. Qualification must cover the intended lighting and neighboring machines rather than treating active illumination as an unconditional range source.

**Indirect time-of-flight (iToF)**\index{Time-of-flight!indirect vs direct} estimates travel time from the phase of modulated reflected light. For quadrature charge samples, the phase relation is:
$$\Delta \phi = \arctan\left(\frac{Q_3 - Q_1}{Q_0 - Q_2}\right)$$
A practical implementation must resolve the quadrant as well as this ratio. The phase yields range, but its periodicity leaves an ambiguity interval; reflected paths in rack corners can mix into a biased depth. Motion between charge samples also corrupts boundary pixels. **Direct time-of-flight (dToF)** instead times discrete photon returns. It avoids this particular phase ambiguity, but receiver timing, overlapping returns, and multipath still require qualification.

**Active stereo**\index{Active stereo!transduction} adds projected texture to a calibrated camera pair. The cameras match that texture using stereo geometry rather than decoding a known projected pattern. When sunlight suppresses the projector, passive image texture may still support matching; a textureless surface does not become measurable merely because ambient illumination is bright. The range-dependent error calculation in @sec-perception-error-clearance decides whether the resulting depth is adequate for clearance.

### Neuromorphic event cameras: Asynchronous temporal contrast

Conventional CMOS sensors integrate photons over a synchronous exposure window, inherently trading motion blur against low-light photon starvation. **Neuromorphic event cameras** (Dynamic Vision Sensors, or DVS)\index{Neuromorphic event cameras!transduction}\index{Event cameras!transduction} abandon discrete frames entirely.

Each pixel on an event sensor array operates autonomously, containing a logarithmic photodiode, an analog amplifier, and two differential voltage comparators. The pixel continuously monitors the incoming scene radiance $I(u, v, t)$. Whenever the temporal change in logarithmic intensity exceeds a configurable contrast threshold $C_{\text{th}}$, the pixel emits an asynchronous digital event packet $e_k$:
$$|\Delta \ln I(u, v, t)| = |\ln I(u, v, t) - \ln I(u, v, t_{\text{last}})| \ge C_{\text{th}}$$
$$e_k = \langle u_k, v_k, t_k, p_k \rangle$$
where $(u_k, v_k)$ is the pixel address, $t_k$ is the event timestamp latched with microsecond resolution ($1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{s}$), and $p_k \in \{-1, +1\}$ is the polarity indicating whether radiance increased or decreased.

Event sensing preserves the timing of changing edges without waiting for a full image exposure and readout, making it useful for rapid motion. The trade-off is that unchanged appearance provides little direct evidence: a stationary obstacle need not generate a useful event stream, while noise and illumination flicker can generate events even without object motion. Link load therefore depends on scene activity and sensor behavior rather than a fixed frame size.

Downstream estimation must turn asynchronous points in $(u, v, t)$ space into a usable temporal representation. Accumulating events into slices permits conventional processing but adds collection delay; processing their individual timestamps preserves timing at the cost of a more complex estimator. Neither choice supplies metric depth by itself.

### Active LiDAR and radar ranging transduction

While optical cameras capture dense angular projections of ambient illumination, active ranging sensors—principally Light Detection and Ranging (**LiDAR**)\index{LiDAR!transduction physics} and Radio Detection and Ranging (**radar**)\index{Radar!FMCW transduction}—emit structured electromagnetic energy and measure its reflection, directly extracting metric depth and radial velocity.

Pulsed time-of-flight LiDAR calculates radial distance $R$ by measuring the round-trip flight duration $\Delta t$ of an emitted laser pulse traveling at the speed of light $c$:
$$R = \frac{c \cdot \Delta t}{2}$$

In three-dimensional space, optical scanners steer each pulse along azimuth $\theta$ and elevation $\phi$, casting an emitted ray along unit direction vector $\mathbf{d}(\theta, \phi) = [\cos\phi\cos\theta, \; \cos\phi\sin\theta, \; \sin\phi]^\top$. When reflected energy trips the receiver threshold after flight time $\Delta t$, the sensor unprojects the return into a 3D point in the sensor frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{lidar}}$ via ray casting (@eq-percep-lidar-ray):
$$\mathbf{p}_{\text{lidar}} = R \cdot \mathbf{d}(\theta, \phi) = \frac{c \cdot \Delta t}{2} \begin{bmatrix} \cos\phi \cos\theta \\ \cos\phi \sin\theta \\ \sin\phi \end{bmatrix}$$ {#eq-percep-lidar-ray}

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-lidar-sweep
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE MACHINE'S LIDAR: RANGE ERROR AND SWEEP DISTORTION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The LiDAR paragraphs of @sec-perception-transduction-calibration;
# │          reused by the LiDAR age budget and the state-estimation example.
# │
# │ Goal:    Give the OS1-64's datasheet range precision and bias, and size
# │          the motion the base makes during one 20 Hz revolution.
# │ Show:    precision 5-30 mm (1 sigma), accuracy 25 mm; 50 ms sweep; 75 mm
# │          of travel and 25 mrad (1.4 degrees) of yaw across one sweep.
# │ How:     RM.lidar.scan_rate; Ouster OS1 Rev7 datasheet (firmware 3.1)
# │          precision and accuracy (registry), specified in the 1024 x 10 Hz
# │          mode; illustrative yaw rate.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_frequency, fmt_angle, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class LidarSweep:
    """Range error and one-revolution motion distortion for the machine's OS1-64."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    lidar = RM.lidar  # category: datasheet (registry: Ouster OS1-64)
    f_scan = lidar.scan_rate  # category: datasheet (configured 20 Hz mode)
    sigma_r_min = lidar.range_precision_min  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 precision min, 1 sigma, beyond 1 m)
    sigma_r_max = lidar.range_precision_max  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 precision max, 1 sigma, beyond 1 m)
    bias_r = lidar.range_accuracy  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 accuracy, Lambertian targets)
    wavelength = lidar.laser_wavelength  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 laser wavelength)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    omega_yaw = 0.5 * radian / second  # category: illustrative (yaw rate)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_sweep = (1 / f_scan).to(millisecond)
    dx_sweep = (v * t_sweep).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dtheta_sweep = (omega_yaw * t_sweep).to(ureg.milliradian)
    dtheta_sweep_deg = dtheta_sweep.to(ureg.degree)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_scan.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected LiDAR scan rate: {f_scan}")
    check(abs(t_sweep.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected sweep period: {t_sweep}")
    check(abs(dx_sweep.magnitude - 75.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected travel per sweep: {dx_sweep}")
    check(abs(dtheta_sweep.magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected yaw per sweep: {dtheta_sweep}")
    check(wavelength.to(ureg.nanometer).magnitude < 1000, "The OS1-64 emits in the near infrared that silicon detectors sense.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    wavelength_str = fmt(wavelength.to(ureg.nanometer).magnitude, precision=0)
    f_scan_str = fmt_frequency(f_scan, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    sigma_r_min_str = fmt_length(sigma_r_min, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    sigma_r_max_str = fmt_length(sigma_r_max, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    bias_r_str = fmt_length(bias_r, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    t_sweep_str = fmt_latency(t_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dx_sweep_str = fmt_length(dx_sweep, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    omega_yaw_str = fmt(omega_yaw.to(radian / second).magnitude, precision=1)
    dtheta_sweep_str = fmt(dtheta_sweep.magnitude, precision=0)
    dtheta_sweep_deg_str = fmt(dtheta_sweep_deg.magnitude, precision=1)
```

Spatial uncertainty in this unprojected point return decomposes into two distinct physical mechanisms:

1. **Radial uncertainty ($\sigma_R$)**: Governed by receiver discriminator timing jitter $\sigma_{\Delta t}$ and pulse rise-time, $\sigma_R = \frac{c}{2} \sigma_{\Delta t}$ remains approximately constant across range until return signal attenuation lowers photon counts near the detection threshold. The datasheet for the machine's OS1-64 gives a one-standard-deviation precision of `{python} LidarSweep.sigma_r_min_str` to `{python} LidarSweep.sigma_r_max_str` beyond 1 m, and separately an accuracy of `{python} LidarSweep.bias_r_str` on diffuse targets [@ouster2025os1]. The second figure bounds the error of the mean, a bias that averaging does not remove.
2. **Transverse uncertainty ($\sigma_\perp$)**: Governed by optical beam divergence $\delta\theta_{\text{div}}$ and angular encoder quantization $\sigma_\theta$. The laser pulse does not travel as an infinitesimal line, but as an expanding cone. At range $R$, the transverse spot size expands as $\sigma_\perp \approx R \cdot \delta\theta_{\text{div}}$. At $R = 30\,\text{m}$, a $2\,\text{mrad}$ beam divergence illuminates a $60\,\text{mm}$ circular disk, creating mixed returns across surface silhouettes and blurring sharp obstacle edges into spatial uncertainty ellipsoids elongated orthogonal to the line of sight.

Most terrestrial systems operate either at near-infrared wavelengths below $1{,}000\,\text{nm}$, where silicon detectors respond, or at an eye-safe $1{,}550\,\text{nm}$ (permitting higher pulse energies under IEC 60825-1 Class 1 laser regulations). The machine's OS1-64 is of the first kind: it emits at `{python} LidarSweep.wavelength_str` nm as a Class 1 laser product [@ouster2025os1]. Mechanical spinning LiDAR systems rotate an array of 16 to 128 laser diodes and avalanche photodiode (APD) detectors across an internal spindle at $10\text{--}20\,\text{Hz}$ to sweep a $360^\circ$ panoramic point cloud.

Just as rolling-shutter CMOS cameras read out scanlines sequentially, a spinning mechanical LiDAR does *not* capture an instantaneous 3D snapshot. A full $360^\circ$ azimuth sweep takes $T_{\text{sweep}} = 1/f_{\text{scan}}$, which is `{python} LidarSweep.t_sweep_str` for the machine's OS1-64 at its configured `{python} LidarSweep.f_scan_str`. If the robot translates at linear velocity $\mathbf{v}$ and rotates at angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ during this sweep, point measurements recorded at the beginning of the rotation ($\theta = 0^\circ$) and the end of the rotation ($\theta = 360^\circ$) correspond to distinct spatial poses of the sensor origin. At the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.v_str` drive limit and an illustrative `{python} LidarSweep.omega_yaw_str` rad/s yaw, the base moves `{python} LidarSweep.dx_sweep_str` and turns `{python} LidarSweep.dtheta_sweep_str` mrad (`{python} LidarSweep.dtheta_sweep_deg_str`°) within one sweep. The visible artifact is a seam where the end of the sweep meets its start, and a shear across the cloud: a rack upright seen late in the sweep appears displaced from where the same upright was seen early.

Restoring rigid geometric fidelity requires **continuous-time LiDAR de-skewing**\index{LiDAR!point cloud de-skewing}. Each individual point return $\mathbf{p}_i$ is latched with a precise firing epoch $t_i \in [t_{\text{start}}, t_{\text{start}} + T_{\text{sweep}}]$. A pose $\mathbf{T}$ packages a rotation and a translation; composing and inverting poses is developed in @sec-perception-coordinate-chain. Using high-rate (`{python} RollingShutterSkew.f_imu_str`) inertial measurements and the motion estimate, the state estimator obtains the body pose $\mathbf{T}_{wb}(t_i)$. The calibrated mounting transform $\mathbf{T}_{bl}$ maps LiDAR-frame coordinates into the body frame, so $\mathbf{T}_{wl}(t_i)=\mathbf{T}_{wb}(t_i)\mathbf{T}_{bl}$ maps them into the world frame. Each homogeneous point return can then be expressed in the LiDAR frame at the common start epoch $t_{\text{start}}$:
$$\mathbf{p}_i(t_{\text{start}}) = \mathbf{T}_{wl}^{-1}(t_{\text{start}}) \cdot \mathbf{T}_{wl}(t_i) \cdot \mathbf{p}_i(t_i)$$
The resulting de-skewed 3D point cloud—illustrated in @fig-08-lidar-pointcloud—reduces distortion from sensor motion, subject to pose and calibration error. Independently moving objects require their own motion treatment.

::: {#fig-08-lidar-pointcloud fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Registered LiDAR point cloud**: Returns from a 64-beam spinning LiDAR on a moving car, registered into one map over about 18 s as a SLAM estimator tracked the vehicle's trajectory, and shown in orthographic projection colored by return intensity times range. The sharp building edges and vehicles hold only because every return was placed with the pose at its own firing time; a single sweep is far sparser than this aggregate. (Credit: [Daniel L. Lu](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ouster_OS1-64_lidar_point_cloud_of_intersection_of_Folsom_and_Dore_St,_San_Francisco.png) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0)." fig-alt="Dense point cloud of a city street intersection seen from above at an angle, colored from dark blue through magenta to orange, showing parked cars, road markings, building facades, and trees."}
![](images/png/fig08_real_lidar_pointcloud.png){width="100%"}
:::

Flash LiDAR illuminates the scene in one pulse, avoiding the azimuth sweep that creates this distortion. Spreading finite pulse energy over the field of view trades that timing advantage against return strength and range.

Millimeter-wave radar provides a fundamentally distinct active modality, operating at $76\text{--}81\,\text{GHz}$ ($\lambda \approx 3.9\,\text{mm}$). Rather than emitting short impulses, **Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar**\index{Radar!FMCW} continuously transmits linear frequency chirps whose instantaneous frequency ramps across bandwidth $B$ over chirp duration $T_c$ with slope $S = B / T_c$. When the emitted chirp reflects off an obstacle at range $R$, the reflected signal arrives delayed by $\tau = 2R/c$. Mixing the received signal with a replica of the transmitted signal produces an intermediate frequency (IF) beat signal with beat frequency $f_b$:
$$f_b = S \cdot \tau = \frac{2 R B}{c \, T_c}$$
Applying a fast Fourier transform (FFT) along the digitized fast-time samples of each chirp (the **Range-FFT**) directly resolves metric range $R$ without reliance on optical texture or environmental lighting. The physical range resolution is governed by chirp bandwidth:
$$\Delta R = \frac{c}{2B}$$
For a typical $4\,\text{GHz}$ automotive sweep ($77\text{--}81\,\text{GHz}$), FMCW radar achieves a fine range resolution of $\Delta R \approx 3.75\,\text{cm}$.

In multi-channel radar front-ends, the digitized samples organize into a three-dimensional **radar data cube**\index{Radar!data cube}: $N_{\text{samples}}$ fast-time range samples $\times$ $N_{\text{chirps}}$ slow-time chirps $\times$ $N_{\text{channels}}$ virtual receive antenna elements formed by Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) array synthesis. Transforming this raw data cube into a 4D metric point cloud executes across three sequential stages:

1. **Range-FFT (Fast-time processing)**: Evaluated across the $N_{\text{samples}}$ of each chirp to resolve the beat frequency $f_b$ and map reflections into range bins with resolution $\Delta R = c / (2B)$.
2. **Doppler-FFT (Slow-time processing)**: Resolves instantaneous radial velocity $v_r$ at the hardware transducer level via the Doppler effect. When an obstacle possesses nonzero radial velocity relative to the sensor, the round-trip distance changes between successive chirps within a frame, introducing a progressive phase shift $\Delta \phi$ across Range-FFT peaks (@eq-percep-radar-doppler). The following Doppler relations assume negligible idle time, so chirp duration $T_c$ also equals the repetition interval between comparable chirps. With idle time or transmitter interleaving, they require the actual repetition interval instead:
$$\Delta \phi = \frac{4 \pi v_r T_c}{\lambda} \implies v_r = \frac{\lambda \, \Delta \phi}{4 \pi T_c}$$ {#eq-percep-radar-doppler}
Evaluating an FFT across the sequence of $N_{\text{chirps}}$ chirps produces a 2D Range-Doppler map with velocity resolution $\Delta v = \frac{\lambda}{2 N_{\text{chirps}} T_c}$ and maximum unambiguous velocity $v_{\max} = \frac{\lambda}{4 T_c}$. Unlike cameras and LiDAR—which must infer obstacle velocities through multi-frame optical flow or temporal tracking models over tens of milliseconds—FMCW radar measures metric velocity directly from electromagnetic wave interference in a single measurement frame.

3. **Angle-of-Arrival (AoA) estimation (Spatial processing)**: Transmitted waves reflecting off an obstacle arrive at adjacent physical receive antennas with a path-length differential $d_{\text{ant}} \sin\theta$, inducing a spatial phase shift $\Delta \psi = \frac{2 \pi d_{\text{ant}} \sin\theta}{\lambda}$. Evaluating a spatial Angle-FFT across the $N_{\text{channels}}$ virtual array yields the target azimuth angle (@eq-percep-radar-aoa):
$$\theta = \arcsin\left(\frac{\lambda \, \Delta \psi}{2 \pi d_{\text{ant}}}\right)$$ {#eq-percep-radar-aoa}

Articulated motion, such as a coworker's swinging limbs, also creates **micro-Doppler signatures**, frequency sidebands around the torso's radial motion. These supply classification cues alongside range and velocity. Radar's longer wavelength reduces sensitivity to some obscurants that disrupt optical sensing, but useful coverage still depends on target reflectivity, viewing direction, and multipath. It supplies complementary evidence rather than an all-weather guarantee.

### Tactile contact grounding via optical elastomers {#sec-perception-tactile-grounding}

At the gripper, distant range measurements cannot establish contact pressure or slip. The gripper itself may occlude the contact patch. An optical tactile sensor places a compliant, illuminated elastomer on the fingertip and images its deformation from inside the sensor. Surface shading supports a calibrated estimate of local shape; embedded marker motion supplies evidence of shear and incipient slip. Converting those image changes to a contact wrench requires a validated model of the pad, its loading, and its wear.

Tactile evidence can therefore support the contact phase of a grasp, while the camera and range sensors support the approach. The shared obligation is to preserve the acquisition time and calibrated coordinate relation. Neither the modality name nor a dense output array supplies those qualifications.

## Dating and Placing the Measurement {#sec-perception-handoff}

Raw sensor hardware yields electrical measurements such as photodiode voltages, time-of-flight counter values, or capacitive displacements. These unstructured signals differ significantly from the state variables needed for downstream autonomy. An actuator controller cannot track a desired force using a two-dimensional grid of raw pixel intensities, and a trajectory optimizer cannot plan collision-free paths using unorganized time-of-flight returns. Downstream estimation, planning, and memory subsystems require structured representations of physical state, including metric positions, velocities, bounding volumes, surface normals, and semantic classifications. Translating raw sensor streams into these representations is the operational responsibility of the perception pipeline. Rather than dumping raw buffers into unmanaged shared memory, production physical systems structure every sensory output into a typed observation contract. Each observation packet or token sequence it hands over must satisfy three fundamental invariants for downstream software: a capture timestamp, a reference frame, and a qualified uncertainty envelope.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_s.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Sense node."}
*The Sense node: translating raw electromagnetic and optical energy into timestamped, frame-anchored spatial claims.*
:::

The first mandatory property is the **capture timestamp**\index{Capture timestamp!definition} $t_0$, which specifies the temporal midpoint of the physical energy integration window (the effective moment the camera shutter was open or the laser pulse fired). Sensors do not take instantaneous snapshots; a camera integrates photons across an exposure duration, and a mechanical lidar sweeps laser pulses over an azimuth arc across several milliseconds. Downstream state observers and vision-language-action policies require $t_0$ to ground observation tokens into the machine's dynamic equations of motion. The arrival stamp, $t_{\text{recv}}$, marks the moment the operating system kernel completes the direct memory access (DMA) transfer. Half the exposure, readout, transport, and DMA all elapse before that moment, so the arrival offset $\tau_{\text{recv}} = t_{\text{recv}} - t_0$ is never zero, and substituting arrival time for capture time corrupts downstream state estimation and action generation.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-arrival-stamp
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ARRIVAL-TIMESTAMP OFFSET ON THE NAVIGATION CAMERA
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The capture-timestamp paragraph of @sec-perception-handoff.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the error an estimator makes when it dates the navigation
# │          camera's frame at DMA completion instead of at the exposure midpoint.
# │ Show:    26.6 ms from exposure midpoint to DMA completion; 39.9 mm of base
# │          travel at the 1.5 m/s drive limit.
# │ How:     t_recv - t0 = t_exp/2 + t_readout + t_transport + t_dma from
# │          RM.nav_camera and AISLE; displacement via
# │          calc_spatial_information_age_displacement.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class ArrivalStampOffset:
    """Age hidden by an arrival timestamp on the running machine's navigation camera."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: navigation camera)
    t_exp = camera.exposure_time  # category: chosen (configured exposure)
    t_readout = camera.readout_time  # category: datasheet
    t_transport = AISLE.t_transport  # category: illustrative
    t_dma = AISLE.t_dma  # category: illustrative
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_recv = (t_exp / 2 + t_readout + t_transport + t_dma).to(millisecond)
    dx_recv = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(v, tau_recv).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_recv.magnitude - 26.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected arrival offset: {tau_recv}")
    check(abs(dx_recv.magnitude - 39.9) < 0.05, f"Unexpected arrival-stamp displacement: {dx_recv}")
    check(tau_recv < AISLE.perception_age, "Arrival offset must be part of the full observation age")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_recv_str = fmt_latency(tau_recv, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    dx_recv_str = fmt_length(dx_recv, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v.to(meter / second), unit=meter / second, precision=1)
```

At constant velocity $v$, the hidden travel is $\Delta x = v\,\tau_{\text{recv}}$. On the mobile manipulator, the navigation camera's frame completes its DMA transfer `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.tau_recv_str` after the exposure midpoint. An estimator that stamps the frame on arrival therefore dates it that much late, and at the base's `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.v_str` drive limit it pairs the observation with a pose `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.dx_recv_str` beyond the one the camera occupied at capture.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ @Sec-memory-reference-frames adds how these sensor-to-body transforms go stale over time.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-extrinsic-error
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EXTRINSIC ANGLE ERRORS AGAINST THE AISLE'S CLEARANCES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The reference-frame paragraph of @sec-perception-handoff, the
# │          transform-chain paragraph of @sec-perception-error-clearance, and
# │          the calibration takeaway.
# │
# │ Goal:    Tie two lever-arm errors to the stopping budget's terms: an
# │          uncalibrated 1 degree mount error at 15 m against the base's side
# │          clearance, and a 0.005 rad extrinsic shift at 10 m against delta_loc.
# │ Show:    0.26 m, about 1.7x the 0.15 m side clearance; 50 mm, the whole
# │          delta_loc allowance.
# │ How:     Delta_y = d sin(theta); delta_x = z theta; AISLE.side_clearance and
# │          AISLE.delta_loc.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_multiple, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class ExtrinsicErrorBudget:
    """Lever-arm errors from angular mount errors, set against the aisle clearances."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    theta_frame = 1.0 * ureg.degree  # category: illustrative (uncalibrated mount error)
    d_frame = 15.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (detection range)
    theta_ext = 0.005 * radian  # category: illustrative (extrinsic shift after shock)
    z_ext = 10.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (target range)
    side_clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dy_frame = (d_frame * math.sin(theta_frame.to(radian).magnitude)).to(meter)
    dy_over_side = (dy_frame / side_clearance).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    dx_ext = (z_ext * theta_ext.magnitude).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dx_over_loc = (dx_ext / delta_loc).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dy_frame.magnitude - 0.2618) < 0.0005, f"Unexpected 1-degree lever-arm error: {dy_frame}")
    check(dy_frame > side_clearance, "Prose says the 1-degree error exceeds the side clearance")
    check(abs(dx_ext.magnitude - 50.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected extrinsic-shift error: {dx_ext}")
    check(abs(dx_over_loc - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Prose says the extrinsic shift spends all of delta_loc")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    theta_frame_str = fmt(theta_frame.to(ureg.degree).magnitude, precision=0)
    d_frame_str = fmt_length(d_frame, unit=meter, precision=0)
    dy_frame_str = fmt_length(dy_frame, unit=meter, precision=2)
    dy_over_side_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dy_over_side, precision=1)
    side_clearance_str = fmt_length(side_clearance.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    theta_ext_str = fmt(theta_ext.magnitude, precision=3)
    z_ext_str = fmt_length(z_ext, unit=meter, precision=0)
    dx_ext_str = fmt_length(dx_ext, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc.to(ureg.millimeter), unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
```

The second mandatory property is the **reference frame**\index{Reference frame!definition} identifier $\mathcal{F}_{\text{sensor}}$. Every spatial measurement is natively resolved in the local coordinate system of the physical transducer. A camera measures bearing angles relative to its optical center, while a radar measures range and Doppler velocity relative to its antenna array. Downstream trajectory planners and obstacle maps operate in a chassis body frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{body}}$ or an inertial navigation frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{world}}$. Transforming an observation from $\mathcal{F}_{\text{sensor}}$ to $\mathcal{F}_{\text{body}}$ requires applying a rigid-body spatial transformation consisting of a rotation matrix and a translation vector that define the sensor mounting extrinsics (the exact physical location and orientation where the sensor is bolted onto the machine). The frames nest from the globe down to the transducer, $\mathcal{F}_{\text{earth}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{map}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{odom}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{body}} \to \mathcal{F}_{\text{sensor}}$, and every link in that tree carries its own transform and uncertainty (@fig-08-coordinate-frame-tree).

When perception outputs omit the frame identifier or rely on nominal CAD dimensions rather than calibrated physical extrinsics, small angular offsets create large spatial errors that scale with distance. An uncalibrated pitch or yaw error of $\theta =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_frame_str`° on a sensor detecting an object at range $d =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.d_frame_str` induces a transverse position error $\Delta y \approx d \sin\theta$ of `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dy_frame_str`, about `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dy_over_side_mult_str` the `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.side_clearance_str` side clearance the base keeps from the racks, so the planner either steers into the racking or rejects a valid aisle as obstructed.

The third mandatory property is an **uncertainty representation**\index{Uncertainty envelope!definition}, such as covariance $\mathbf{\Sigma}_z$ together with a validated tail or hard error bound when clearance depends on it. Low illumination, atmospheric scattering, specular surfaces, and model error change the residual distribution. A covariance describes second moments, not a region guaranteed to contain the true state. Downstream observers and policy heads can use it to weight sensory innovations against a motion model; an underestimated covariance can pull an estimate toward a spurious measurement and lead to poor downstream commands. Safety decisions must also account for bias, missed detections, and validation limits.

### Calibrating the coordinate chain {#sec-perception-coordinate-chain}

A frame transform answers where a point expressed relative to one origin lies relative to another. Its rotation changes the direction of the coordinate axes, and its translation accounts for the offset between their origins. The matrix notation below packages those operations so the camera-to-wrist, wrist-to-base, and base-to-world mappings can be composed at the observation's capture time. The engineering requirement is that every link describe the physical mounting and pose at that time.

A robot's spatial coordinate frames form a **directed acyclic graph (DAG)** of transforms $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$, where vertices $\mathcal{V} = \{\mathcal{F}_i\}$ represent physical coordinate frames and directed edges $\mathcal{E}$ represent time-varying rigid-body transforms $\mathbf{T}_{ij}(t) \in \text{SE}(3)$. The selected frame tree gives each nonroot frame exactly one parent; a general DAG need not provide a unique path. When unprojecting an optical observation $\mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}(t_0)$ into world coordinates, the runtime composes the transforms along that tree:
$$\mathbf{p}_{\text{world}}(t_0) = \mathbf{T}_{\text{world}}^{\text{map}} \cdot \mathbf{T}_{\text{map}}^{\text{odom}}(t_0) \cdot \mathbf{T}_{\text{odom}}^{\text{base}}(t_0) \cdot \mathbf{T}_{\text{base}}^{\text{flange}}(t_0) \cdot \mathbf{T}_{\text{flange}}^{\text{cam}} \cdot \mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}(t_0)$$
The physical mounting location of the sensor on the kinematic chain dictates how coordinate transforms update across this DAG:

In an **eye-in-hand**\index{Eye-in-hand calibration!definition} configuration, the camera or depth sensor is bolted directly to the manipulator's moving tool flange ($\mathcal{F}_{\text{flange}}$). Moving any preceding joint alters the sensor's optical center relative to the world, requiring continuous forward kinematics updates. Solving for the rigid extrinsic transform $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{T}_{\text{flange}}^{\text{cam}} \in \text{SE}(3)$ requires executing robot motions across $N \ge 2$ non-parallel rotational axes while observing a stationary fiducial target (such as a ChArUco grid). For two distinct poses $k$ and $k+1$, the closed kinematic loop establishes the classic **hand-eye matrix equation**:
$$\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{B}$$
where $\mathbf{A} = (\mathbf{T}_{\text{base}, k}^{\text{flange}})^{-1} \mathbf{T}_{\text{base}, k+1}^{\text{flange}} \in \text{SE}(3)$ is the relative flange displacement reported by the forward kinematics chain, and $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T}_{\text{cam}, k}^{\text{target}} (\mathbf{T}_{\text{cam}, k+1}^{\text{target}})^{-1} \in \text{SE}(3)$ is the relative camera displacement extracted from optical target unprojection.

In an **eye-to-hand**\index{Eye-to-hand calibration!definition} calibration rig, the camera overlooks the workspace from a body-mounted mast or a stationary overhead beam. The base must remain parked relative to an overhead camera during calibration. Under that condition, the camera-to-base transform remains constant ($\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{T}_{\text{base}}^{\text{cam}} \in \text{SE}(3)$), while the target is affixed to the robot's moving end-effector ($\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{T}_{\text{flange}}^{\text{target}} \in \text{SE}(3)$). At each joint configuration, let $\mathbf{A}=(\mathbf{T}_{\text{base}}^{\text{flange}})^{-1}$ map base coordinates into the flange frame and $\mathbf{B}=(\mathbf{T}_{\text{cam}}^{\text{target}})^{-1}$ map camera coordinates into the target frame. These are absolute pose transforms for this rig, not the relative motions used above. Both paths then map camera coordinates into the flange frame:
$$\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{Z} \mathbf{B}$$
If the mobile base later moves relative to the overhead camera, its camera-to-base transform must change accordingly.

Treating the nominal rigid transform chain from CAD as an exact physical calibration ignores load and temperature effects. Physical manipulators exhibit mechanical compliance under payload mass, lost motion and torsional wind-up in the joints (strain wave gears have near-zero backlash, but their flexsplines still twist under load), and thermal expansion (structural aluminum expands at $\alpha \approx 23 \times 10^{-6}/\text{K}$). For an illustrative $1\,\text{meter}$ aluminum link that warms uniformly by $10^\circ\text{C}$, the corresponding expansion is $0.23\,\text{mm}$. A motor temperature rise alone does not establish that link-temperature change; actual thermal gradients and encoder shifts require measurement before updating the calibration.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-wrist-timestamp-skew
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ JOINT-TO-CAMERA TIMESTAMP SKEW AT THE WRIST
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The joint-kinematics timing paragraph of
# │          @sec-perception-coordinate-chain.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the wrist-camera error from a joint/camera timestamp skew and
# │          the largest skew a grasp tolerance allows.
# │ Show:    10 mm + 3 mm = 13 mm for a 10 ms skew; 3.8 ms allowed for 5 mm.
# │ How:     dp = (v + omega r) dt; dt_max = eps_pos / (v + omega r).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

class WristTimestampSkew:
    """Wrist-camera position error from joint/camera timestamp skew."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_wrist = 1.0 * meter / second  # category: illustrative (wrist linear speed)
    omega_wrist = 2.0 * radian / second  # category: illustrative (wrist angular speed)
    r_cam = 0.15 * meter  # category: illustrative (camera lever arm)
    dt_skew = 10.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (unmodeled skew)
    eps_pos = 5.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (grasp position tolerance)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_eff = (v_wrist + omega_wrist.to(1 / second).magnitude * r_cam / second).to(meter / second)
    dp_lin = (v_wrist * dt_skew).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dp_rot = ((v_eff - v_wrist) * dt_skew).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dp = (dp_lin + dp_rot).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dt_max = (eps_pos / v_eff).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dp.magnitude - 13.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected skew error: {dp}")
    check(abs(dt_max.magnitude - 3.85) < 0.01, f"Unexpected skew bound: {dt_max}")
    check(dt_max > 1.0 * millisecond, "Prose says millisecond-level alignment suffices")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
```
